stupefy

/STOO-puh-fye/ - the stress falls on STOO · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Stupefy means to stun someone into dazed amazement.

The final round of the memory championship stupefied the audience: the winner recited two hundred digits without a pause.

Example

The auction house expected the little sketch to fetch a modest sum; the final bid — forty-two million — stupefied even the auctioneer, who stood with his gavel raised for a long, silent moment.

Stupefy is stronger than surprise or impress: it stuns the mind into a daze, so that for a moment thought and speech simply stop. Its cousin 'stupor' names that same frozen state.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

daze: Daze means to leave someone unable to think straight, whatever the cause — a blow to the head, exhaustion, shocking news. Stupefy is a daze with a signature cause: amazement so overwhelming it stalls the mind. Every stupefied person is dazed; a boxer can be dazed with no amazement at all.

dumbfound: Dumbfound means to astonish someone so completely that speech fails — the mouth opens and nothing comes out. Stupefy freezes thought rather than speech: a stupefied person can still talk, even babble, while the mind refuses to work. Dumbfounded is speechless; stupefied is dazed.

stun: Stun means to shock someone so hard that reaction stops for an instant — bad news, a blow, a blinding flash. Stupefy lasts longer and centers on amazement: a stunned person recovers in a beat, while a stupefied one stays foggy long after the shock lands.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

bore: to dull someone's interest entirely

underwhelm: to impress far less than expected

Where it sits · how completely it knocks out thought — surprise → astonish → stupefy

surprise vs. stupefy: A surprise merely catches you off guard — a friend at the door; it is far milder than stupefy, which stops thought altogether.

astonish vs. stupefy: Astonish is strong — jaws drop — but it stops short of stupefy, which leaves its victims dazed, unable for a moment to think or speak.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — stup-

Root — stup-: stunned, dazed (Latin stupere, 'to be struck senseless')

Suffix — -efy

Suffix — -efy: to make (a spelling of -ify)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin stupere means 'to be struck senseless with amazement,' and -efy — the same maker-suffix as -ify, wearing its other spelling — turns it into 'to make senseless.' The root fans out from there: a stupor is the dazed state itself, and something stupendous is literally 'worth being stunned by.'

Use the root in a new word: stupor

Use the root in a new word: stupor: The chart recorded the patient's stupor in two clipped words.

Word Choice

formal / vivid

Use stupefy when amazement (or exhaustion, or a drug) genuinely stalls the mind — it is stronger than astonish and more physical than amaze. In this unit it makes a tidy contrast with demystify: one word clears a head, the other stops one.
